//: Tomato and potato. Agronomic entries are scoped by deviceNamePattern to placeholders (%tomato%, %potato%) — rename devices to match or replace the pattern with deviceProfiles before trusting an alert. Thresholds are the published extension figures cited in each entry; they are starting points, not calibrations.
//months: activeMonths are Central Valley processing-tomato timing (transplant March–May, fruit set June–August) and California potato timing. Shift them for your planting dates.
//enabled: Enabled: checks whose threshold is a published figure the sensor measures directly — air, leaf and soil temperature, humidity, durations, rates, pH. Disabled: checks whose threshold depends on this soil or this probe (volumetric moisture, EC, N, the 'wet' cut-off of a leaf-wetness sensor) or that need the forecast block — each says what to set before enabling it.

checks.//: ═══ FLEET HEALTH — every pack carries these, so the pack runs on its own. None needs crop tuning. ═══

LATE BLIGHT (Phytophthora infestans) — the Smith Period: "two consecutive days where the minimum temperature is not below 10°C and there are at least 11 hours each day with a relative humidity ≥90%" (Dancey et al. 2017). The hours are a total per day, not one unbroken run. The UK now uses the Hutton criteria, the same with ≥ 6 h — the second, disabled entry per crop. Days here run 09:00 to 09:00 local (dayStartHour 9), so one humid night stays inside one day. The published definitions give no day boundary; UK practice uses the Met Office 09:00–09:00 GMT climatological day (Bayer UK states "ending at 0900 hours"), and 09:00 local keeps that intent — 09:00 GMT would be 01:00 in California. A midnight day (dayStartHour 0) splits each night across two days, so it is less sensitive and later, most at the start of a short spell. The criteria were built on Met Office screen stations; an in-canopy RH sensor usually reads wetter, so expect more alerts. UC IPM notes Smith "may not be directly usable under California conditions"; US programmes use Wallin severity values (BLITECAST) — the disabled -wallin entries below. Sources: Dancey et al. 2017, https://euroblight.net/fileadmin/euroblight/Workshops/AArhus/Proceedings/5._Siobhan_Dancy-p53-58.pdf ; Met Office MIDAS guide, https://artefacts.ceda.ac.uk/badc_datadocs/ukmo-midas/ukmo_guide.html ; UC IPM, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/DISEASE/DATABASE/potatolateblight.html

LATE BLIGHT — Wallin severity values, the model BLITECAST builds on and the one most US late-blight programmes use. Each day earns 0–4 from its hours at RH ≥ 90 % and the mean temperature during them (UC IPM table, 7.2–26.6 °C); accumulation starts at plant emergence, and blight is predicted 7–14 days after 18–20 severity values, so the first spray is due at 18. After a spray point the count restarts from zero. BLITECAST times later sprays from a seven-day matrix of rain-favourable days and severity values, which needs rainfall and is not implemented — treat repeat alerts as an approximation of it. Validated in the eastern US; UC IPM lists no model validated for California. DISABLED: set since to the field's emergence date (YYYY-MM-DD) before enabling. Source: UC IPM, potato late blight models, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/DISEASE/DATABASE/potatolateblight.html

═══ FRUIT SET ═══ Rutgers and UMD: days above 32 °C (90 °F) together with nights above 21 °C (70 °F) reduce tomato fruit set; nights below 13 °C (55 °F) cause blossom drop. The optimum night is 15–21 °C. Sources: Rutgers, https://plant-pest-advisory.rutgers.edu/high-temperatures-and-effect-on-tomato-pollination-and-fruit-set/ ; UMD, https://extension.umd.edu/resource/expect-poor-fruit-set-tomatoes-week

BLOSSOM-END ROT RISK — root-zone moisture swinging instead of holding steady. UC IPM: keep root-zone moisture uniform and do not let the soil dry during fruit growth; salinity and sandy soils make it worse. No source gives a numeric swing, so the alert to watch is this rule's "oscillating" classification, not a threshold. DISABLED: floor and ceiling are placeholders — set them to this probe's readings at ~40 % depletion (FAO-56 p for tomato is 0.40) and at field capacity. Sources: UC IPM, "Blossom-end rot", https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/GARDEN/VEGES/ENVIRON/blossomendrot.html ; FAO-56 Table 22, https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e0e.htm

═══ POTATO ═══ NDSU: tuber optimum is 15–20 °C; tuberization falls when nights exceed 20 °C and stops above 25 °C; soil at 24 °C (75 °F) can start second growth, and 28 °C for a month or 32 °C for a week gives it consistently. Source: NDSU, "Potato tuber second growth", https://ag.ndsu.edu/publications/crops/potato-tuber-second-growth
28 °C held half a day at tuber depth. NDSU's consistent-second-growth figure is 28 °C for a month; this raises at the start of such a spell rather than a month in.

COMMON SCAB. NDSU: scab is suppressed at pH ≤ 5.2; risk spans 5.2–8.0 and is worst when soil is dry during the first 3–6 weeks after tuber initiation. This is info — it says the field is in the risk range, which makes keeping the soil moist through tuber initiation the lever. Source: NDSU, "Common scab", https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/potatoextension/common-scab

ROOT-ZONE SALINITY — tomato: Maas–Hoffman threshold ECe 2.5 dS/m, above which yield declines. DISABLED until converted to what the probe reads. Maas–Hoffman thresholds are saturated-paste ECe. A soil probe reports bulk EC (or pore EC), which is not ECe: FAO 29 gives soil-water EC ≈ 2 × ECe at field capacity, and bulk EC is lower than pore EC and moves with water content. Convert before enabling — take a saturated-paste lab sample beside the probe and scale this threshold by the probe/ECe ratio. Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, ch. 2 and Annex 1 (Maas & Grattan 1999), https://www.fao.org/4/t0234e/t0234e02.htm , https://www.fao.org/4/y4263e/y4263e0e.htm

ROOT-ZONE SALINITY — potato: Maas–Hoffman threshold ECe 1.7 dS/m, above which yield declines. DISABLED until converted to what the probe reads. Maas–Hoffman thresholds are saturated-paste ECe. A soil probe reports bulk EC (or pore EC), which is not ECe: FAO 29 gives soil-water EC ≈ 2 × ECe at field capacity, and bulk EC is lower than pore EC and moves with water content. Convert before enabling — take a saturated-paste lab sample beside the probe and scale this threshold by the probe/ECe ratio. Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, ch. 2 and Annex 1 (Maas & Grattan 1999), https://www.fao.org/4/t0234e/t0234e02.htm , https://www.fao.org/4/y4263e/y4263e0e.htm

SOIL pH — tomato: outside 6.0–6.8. pH moves over seasons, not hours, so this is info and needs a day sustained; it stays open until the field is limed or acidified. Source: Wisconsin A2809, https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/nutrient-application-guidelines-for-field-vegetable-and-fruit-crops-in-wisconsin-a2809/soil-ph-and-lime-requirement/

═══ TOM-CAST ═══ Early blight, Septoria leaf spot and black mold. Each day earns a disease severity value (0–4) from its hours of leaf wetness and the mean temperature during them; spray when the total since the last spray reaches the threshold — UC IPM's black-mold program uses 12 DSV for susceptible varieties and 18 for resistant (15 is the Midwest default), from July 1 or first fruit color until 7–10 days before harvest. Each crossing raises an alert and resets the count to zero — DSV earned on the crossing day beyond the threshold is not carried into the next interval, matching UC IPM's "each time 12 DSVs or 18 DSVs have accumulated" after a spray. Source: UC IPM, tomato black mold models, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/DISEASE/DATABASE/tomatoblackmold.html
On a leaf-wetness sensor, which is what the model was built on. DISABLED: wetMin 50 is a placeholder for this sensor's wet cut-off.

The same model with hours at RH ≥ 90 % standing in for leaf wetness, for blocks with only a climate sensor — the proxy the humidity-based disease entries in these packs all use. Prefer the wetness-sensor entry where one is installed, and disable this one.
